## Short answer
FY2025-26 is not a loss year: Refex's standalone PAT rose 30% to ₹246 crore on a turnover that fell to ₹2,075 crore from ₹2,430 crore after exiting power trading and refrigerants [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55]. The core worry is not earnings but working capital and off-balance-sheet exposure: receivables plus contract assets in coal/ash handling equal 58.34% of assets and are a key audit matter [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.183][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.266], and corporate guarantees to subsidiaries and others jumped to ₹54,685.45 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261]. Ratings were reaffirmed with a stable outlook (ACUITE A-/A2+) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.121], and the auditors gave a clean opinion with no going-concern or statutory-dues default flags [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.70][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.194].

## Profitability and revenue
- Standalone turnover fell to ₹2,075 crore from ₹2,430 crore, mainly from discontinuing low-margin power trading and refrigerant businesses [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55].
- Standalone PBT rose 38.17% to ₹333 crore and standalone PAT rose 30% to ₹246 crore versus ₹189 crore [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55].
- Consolidated turnover was ₹2,412 crore versus ₹2,468 crore; consolidated PBT rose 39% to ₹277 crore and consolidated PAT 29% to ₹204 crore [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.56].
- Discontinuing operations produced a loss: PBT of ₹(5,295.93) lakh and PAT of ₹(3,866.18) lakh for FY2025-26 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.345]; the refrigerant business was discontinued by Board approval on January 21, 2026 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.203] and power trading earlier [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.84].

## Leverage, liquidity and working capital
- Standalone net debt is nil, with cash and equivalents of ₹18,047.60 lakh exceeding total debt of ₹15,890.59 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.249]; short-term borrowings rose to ₹13,280.95 lakh from ₹6,001.86 lakh and long-term borrowings fell to ₹2,609.65 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.197].
- The current ratio declined on higher current liabilities, and receivable turnover fell with debtor days rising; net capital turnover declined as working capital grew faster than turnover [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.259].
- Trade receivables rose to ₹73,730.89 lakh from ₹67,363.31 lakh, and contract assets surged to ₹73,413.62 lakh from ₹17,143.66 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.197].
- Coal and ash handling trade receivables plus contract assets were ₹1,41,320.12 lakh, about 58.34% of total assets, with ECL allowance only ₹87.13 lakh against gross receivables of ₹88,712.26 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.183][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.303].

## Ratings
- Acuité Ratings & Research reaffirmed on January 08, 2026: long-term bank facilities ACUITE A-: Stable and short-term cash credit ACUITE A2+ [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.76][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.121].

## Related party, guarantees and contingencies
- Related party transactions were at arm's length and in the ordinary course; no material conflicting transaction [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.70][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.121].
- Corporate guarantees total ₹54,685.45 lakh (₹8,375.45 lakh prior year), including ₹45,706.00 lakh for Venwind Refex Power and ₹3,748.00 lakh for other companies; loans and advances to related parties were ₹13,416.42 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].
- An inter-corporate deposit of ₹4,500.00 lakh was placed with Rudra Securities and Capital Limited [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.224][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].
- Contingent liabilities from direct/indirect tax and other claims are a key audit matter [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.184][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.267]; the consolidated contingent liability note carries balances of ₹2,84,269.92 lakh vs ₹1,79,918.97 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.339].
- Pending tax demands include ₹4,628.17 lakh (AY2019-20) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324], ₹4,086.66 lakh (AY2020-21) and ₹1,136.78 lakh (AY2021-22) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.323]; litigation includes a ₹3,567.21 lakh demand, later quashed by the Madras High Court on 28-04-2026 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324].

## Auditor and cash-flow matters
- The auditors issued an unmodified true-and-fair-view opinion on standalone and consolidated statements [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.181][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.264], with no qualification, reservation or adverse remark and no frauds reported [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.70].
- No default in repayment of loans or interest, no willful-defaulter declaration, and short-term funds not used for long-term purposes [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.194]; cash-loss reporting is negative [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.195].
- No material uncertainty on meeting liabilities falling due within one year [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.195]; going-concern language is auditor boilerplate with no reported material uncertainty [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.186][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.268].

Aspect not addressed by the evidence: a specific debt-equity or current-ratio figure for FY2025-26 (only direction of change is given) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.259].

chunks.text: During the year under review, the Company achieved a standalone turnover of ₹2,075 crore as against ₹2,430 crore during the previous year. The movement in revenue was mainly on account of the discontinuation of the Power Trading & Refrigerant business during the year, which were relatively low- margin in nature. Despite the reduction in top line, the Company delivered a significantly stronger operating performance, supported by improvement in margins across its core business operations. Your Company has reported a profit before tax (PBT) of ₹333 crore for the year under review as compared to PBT of ₹241 crore for the previous year on a standalone basis, which is an upside of 38.17%. Your Company has reported a profit after tax (PAT) of ₹246 crore as against a profit after tax of ₹189 crore during the previous year on a standalone basis, which is an upside of 30%.

The recognition of contract assets requires significant management judgement, particularly in measuring quantities of ash disposed, and obtaining customer certification for work completed. Unbilled revenue and price variations are recognized based on contractual terms and quantity disposed based on the DPR prepared by the management. Estimation is involved in ascertaining sale quantity for unbilled revenue as the UOM considered for billing is different from the UOM adopted in the DPR. Daily Progress Report (DPR) is prepared by the management, recording the quantum of ash disposal made site-wise. Furthermore, the Company evaluates trade receivables for expected credit losses (ECL) using a provision matrix. This involves assessing customer credit risk, payment history, and applying historical loss rates adjusted for current and forecasted economic conditions. Due to the significant estimates and assumptions involved in determining the recoverability of contract assets and measuring the ECL on trade receivables of Ash and Coal Handling Business, we have identified this area as a key audit matter. Financial Reports as at and for the year ended March Refex Industries Limited (REFEX) is a specialist manufacturer and re-filler of Refrigerant gases, particularly, environmentally acceptable gases that are replacements for Chloro-Fluoro-Carbons (CFC’s). These are used primarily as refrigerants, foam blowing agents and aerosol propellants. It exercises superior quality control and efficiency with the help of advanced technology. Refex has been committed to being an exemplary player in terms of safety, protection of health and environment, and sustainable development. The Board of Directors approved the discontinuation of the Refrigerant Gases business segment at its meeting held on January 21, 2026. As a result, the activity qualifies as a discontinued operation under Ind AS 105. Accordingly, the Company has disclosed the profit from discontinuing operations separately from the profit from continuing operations in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

4.The Board, at its meeting held on August 12, 2025, has approved the discontinuation of Power Trading business segment. The segment has not been a significant profit driver for the Company with low volumes, lower margins, high compliance costs, and limited strategic fit with the core logistics and energy infrastructure strengths. This process includes surrendering the trading license, settling all statutory obligations, and transparently communicating the rationale for exiting to key stakeholders. 5.A wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company, namely Refex Mobility Limited, was incorporated on September 12, 2025, pursuant to the approval granted by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. 6.Venwind Refex Projects Limited was incorporated as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Venwind Refex Power Limited (VRPL), on November 25, 2025. As on March 31, 2026, the Company holds 77.39% of the equity shares of Venwind Refex Projects Limited indirectly. Subsequent to the close of the financial year, the Company is holding 73.28% indirectly. 7.Refex Engineering Products Private Limited (REPPL) was acquired and made a wholly-owned subsidiary of Venwind Refex Power Limited (VRPL), on December 05, 2025, from Refex Holding Private Limited through secondary transfer of equity shares. As on March 31, 2026, the Company holds 77.39% of the equity shares of REPPL indirectly. Subsequent to the close of the financial year, the Company is holding 73.28% indirectly.

chunks.section: Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements
chunks.text: • Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated Ind AS financial statements, whether due to fraud or error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control. • Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances. Under section 143(3)(i) of the Act, we are also responsible for expressing our opinion on whether the Holding Company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls. • Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting estimates and related disclosures made by management. • Conclude on the appropriateness of management's use of the going concern basis of accounting and, based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material uncertainty exists related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern. ## Short answer
Group exposure is dominated by a single off-balance-sheet item: corporate guarantees for subsidiaries, which rose from Rs 4,627.45 lakh at March 31, 2025 to Rs 50,937.45 lakh at March 31, 2026 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.255][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.340]. On balance sheet, loans and investments in subsidiaries also grew, but the related-party share of loans and advances and of investments fell from 100% in FY2024-25 to 0% in FY2025-26 on the BRR metric [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.145].

## Off-balance-sheet guarantees
- Corporate Guarantee for Subsidiary: Rs 50,937.45 lakh at March 31, 2026 vs Rs 4,627.45 lakh at March 31, 2025 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.255][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.340].
- Corporate Guarantee for Group Co.: nil in both years; Other Corporate Guarantees Rs 3,748.00 lakh in both years [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.255][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.340].
- Note 43 gives the split: Refex Green Mobility Rs 5,231.45 lakh (PY Rs 4,627.45 lakh) and Venwind Refex Power Rs 45,706.00 lakh (PY nil); total guarantees Rs 54,685.45 lakh vs Rs 8,375.45 lakh, including Rs 3,748.00 lakh for other companies [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].

## Balance-sheet group exposure (standalone, Note 43)
- Investments: RGML Rs 8,000.00 lakh (unchanged), Venwind Refex Power Rs 10,299.84 lakh (PY nil); total Rs 18,600.84 lakh vs Rs 8,306.70 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].
- Loans and advances: RGML Rs 8,277.50 lakh (PY Rs 1,427.00 lakh), VRPL Rs 3,697.00 lakh (PY nil), plus Rs 4,500.00 lakh to Rudra Securities (non-group); total Rs 13,416.42 lakh vs Rs 5,124.00 lakh [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].
- Loans and advances to subsidiaries of Rs 4,500.00 lakh carry 9% interest and are given to Venwind Refex Power Limited [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.224].

## Related-party share and group structure
- BRR metric: loans & advances to related parties/total 0% (FY2025-26) vs 100% (FY2024-25); investments in related parties/total 0% vs 100%; sales to related parties 0.08% vs 0.35% [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.145].
- Group: Refex Holding Private Limited holds 55.85% as of March 31, 2026 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.64][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.306]; subsidiaries include Refex Green Mobility (WOS), Refex EV Fleet Services (step-down WOS), Refex Mobility (WOS, incorporated September 12, 2025), and Venwind Refex Power (77.39% held as of March 31, 2026, 73.28% post year-end) plus its step-down entities [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.64][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.65][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.84].
- Transactions with VRPL during FY2025-26 included loans and advances, interest income on loans and OCDs, corporate guarantees, investments and lease/rental income [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.81].
- The statutory auditor states investments, guarantees and loans/advances to companies are not prejudicial to the company's interests, with the subsidiaries/associates amounts tabulated [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.192].

answer:
## Short answer

FY2024-25's interest coverage (2.30x) and DSCR (2.24x) were crushed by a one-time interest payment to HSIIDC that took finance costs from Rs. 0.93 Lakhs to Rs. 237.41 Lakhs; with that gone (Rs. 1.41 Lakhs in FY2025-26), coverage and DSCR mechanically jump to 227.02x and 211.18x [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2025 p.37][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.89]. Underlying debt service actually weakened: borrowings more than doubled, debt-equity rose from 0.04 to 0.08, EBITDA fell, and operating cash flow turned negative [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.91][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.37].

## Reported debt-service metrics

- Interest coverage: 2.30x in FY2024-25 vs 227.02x in FY2025-26; management attributes the increase to lower finance cost [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2025 p.37].
- DSCR: 2.24x in FY2024-25 vs 211.18x in FY2025-26, "improved due to reduction in Interest Cost" [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110].
- Debt-equity: 0.04x in FY2024-25 vs 0.08x in FY2025-26, up 111.53%, "due to increase in debts of the company" [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110].
- FY2024-25's collapse was itself a one-off: the prior year (FY2023-24) DSCR was 327.62x and coverage 345.49x, "decreased due to one time payment of interest cost to HSIIDC" [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2025 p.37].

## What drove it

- Finance costs fell from Rs. 237.41 Lakhs to Rs. 1.41 Lakhs (interest Rs. 234.60 Lakhs to Rs. 1.41 Lakhs) [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.89][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.107].
- Profit before finance cost fell from Rs. 545.20 Lakhs to Rs. 320.10 Lakhs, so the EBIT base shrank while the denominator collapsed [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.37].
- Revenue from operations declined to Rs. 14,897.55 Lakhs from Rs. 16,025.02 Lakhs; total income Rs. 14,981.39 Lakhs vs Rs. 16,099.80 Lakhs [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.89][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.7].
- Profit before tax rose marginally to Rs. 318.69 Lakhs from Rs. 307.78 Lakhs; PAT Rs. 239.97 Lakhs vs Rs. 236.96 Lakhs [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.89].
- EBITDA margin fell to 2.53% from 3.78%, "due to lower operating profit margin" [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.39].
- Management cites challenging steel-market conditions, competition, raw-material price volatility, subdued end-user demand and the Iran/Middle East conflict affecting energy, freight and raw-material prices [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.7].

## Leverage and cash flow

- Total borrowings rose to Rs. 352.11 Lakhs from Rs. 159.64 Lakhs; adjusted net debt Rs. 327.82 Lakhs vs Rs. 137.91 Lakhs against total equity of Rs. 4,397.00 Lakhs vs Rs. 4,216.96 Lakhs [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110].
- Borrowings are entirely current, secured working capital limits from a bank, secured by hypothecation of receivables and inventory, mortgage of land, buildings and plant & machinery, and personal guarantees of the Whole Time Director and Managing Director [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.103].
- Net cash from operating activities was negative Rs. 115.84 Lakhs in FY2025-26 versus positive Rs. 569.06 Lakhs in FY2024-25 [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.91].
- FY2025-26 financing included Rs. 192.47 Lakhs of new overdraft borrowings and a Rs. 73.27 Lakhs dividend, versus interest paid of Rs. 237.41 Lakhs in the prior year [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.91].
- The Company reported no default in interest payment or loan repayment, and Acuite reaffirmed 'ACUITE BBB'/'ACUITE A3+' with a Stable outlook [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.10].

## Comparability

- No restatement or accounting-policy change affecting the comparison is disclosed; FY2025-26 notes only that prior-year figures were regrouped/reclassified where necessary, and that the New Labour Codes' impact was assessed as not material [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.113].

chunks.text: During the financial year under review, the Company recorded revenue from operations of Rs. 14,897.55 Lakhs as compared to Rs. 16,025.02 Lakhs in the previous financial year. The decline in revenue during the year was primarily attributable to relatively challenging market conditions prevailing in the steel industry, including increased competition, volatility in raw material and steel prices, pressure on margins, and subdued demand from certain end-user sectors. The industry also witnessed fluctuations in domestic and global market dynamics, which impacted overall sales volumes during the year. In addition, the ongoing conflict in Iran and the Middle East caused problems in global energy supply, higher freight and shipping costs, and changes in international raw material prices during the year. This also disturbed the movement of steel and raw materials across global markets, adding further uncertainty to the industry. Although the Company mainly operates in the domestic market, these global issues still had an effect on overall demand within the domestic steel industry, which impacted sales and turnover during the year. Despite these challenges, the Company continued to focus on maintaining customer relationships, operational efficiency and market presence. Further, the Company reported profit before tax of Rs. 239.97 Lakhs for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, as against Rs. 236.96 Lakhs in the previous year, reflecting a marginal growth in profitability. The improvement in profit was supported by effective cost optimization measures, improved operational efficiencies, and focused resource management initiatives undertaken by the Company.

answer:
## Short answer
Bhadora Industries' FY2024-25 growth was funded heavily by external debt rather than internal accruals: operating cash flow was only Rs. 351.68 lakhs against Rs. 1,014.93 lakhs of net profit, while financing inflows were Rs. 248.36 lakhs after fresh long-term borrowings of Rs. 366.22 lakhs and short-term borrowing proceeds of Rs. 653.39 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.72][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.5]. Receivables quality deteriorated sharply — trade receivables nearly doubled to Rs. 2,177.41 lakhs and the receivable turnover ratio collapsed 83.26% to 1.62 [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.41][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.76]. Liquidity is adequate but thin, with a current ratio of 1.59 and debt-equity of 0.94 [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.81].

## Funding of growth
- Operating cash flow post working-capital changes was Rs. 351.68 lakhs versus profit before tax of Rs. 1,385.51 lakhs, with the gap driven by a Rs. 957.75 lakhs receivables build [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.72].
- Financing activities generated Rs. 248.36 lakhs net, including long-term borrowing proceeds of Rs. 366.22 lakhs and short-term borrowing proceeds of Rs. 653.39 lakhs, partly offset by finance costs paid of Rs. 277.77 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.72].
- Capex consumed Rs. 729.95 lakhs of investing outflow, with net cash used in investing of Rs. 845.17 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.72].
- The IPO of 54,00,000 equity shares at Rs. 103 each raised Rs. 5,562.00 lakhs, with listing on NSE Emerge effective August 11, 2025 [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.21][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.34].
- Revenue grew to Rs. 11,011.18 lakhs from Rs. 8,139.32 lakhs, and PAT to Rs. 1,014.93 lakhs from Rs. 501.79 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.40].

## Receivables quality
- Trade receivables rose to Rs. 2,177.41 lakhs from Rs. 1,219.65 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.76].
- Of the Rs. 2,177.41 lakhs, Rs. 1,997.61 lakhs were under 6 months, Rs. 96.26 lakhs in 1-2 years, Rs. 38.63 lakhs in 2-3 years and Rs. 8.79 lakhs over 3 years [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.76].
- The trade receivable turnover ratio fell to 1.62 from 9.68, an 83.26% decline attributed to the increase in trade receivables [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.41].

## Working capital and liquidity
- Current ratio was 1.59 (prior year 1.55); debt-equity was 0.94 (prior year 0.89) [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.81][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.41].
- Inventories were Rs. 981.42 lakhs (prior year Rs. 829.20 lakhs) and inventory turnover improved to 12.16 from 9.13 [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.70][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.41].
- Cash and cash equivalents were Rs. 276.50 lakhs versus Rs. 28.14 lakhs a year earlier [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.70].
- Trade payables were Rs. 416.41 lakhs, and payables turnover rose to 19.21 from 14.80 on quicker settlement [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.75][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.41].

## Lender exposure and debt service
- Short-term borrowings were Rs. 1,483.29 lakhs (prior year Rs. 829.89 lakhs) and long-term borrowings Rs. 483.35 lakhs (prior year Rs. 117.13 lakhs) [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.70].
- Debt service coverage ratio was 5.06 and return on equity 0.49 [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.81].
- Bank limits include a Rs. 1,000 lakhs ICICI CC limit at repo plus 2.5%, a Rs. 200 lakhs Indian Bank overdraft at 9.75% secured on stock and book debts, and a SIDBI equipment loan of Rs. 539 lakhs [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.74].
- Quarterly stock/debtor statements filed with ICICI Bank showed material variations from books (e.g. Rs. 307.58 lakhs in September), attributed to timing and clerical differences [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.64][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.80].
- Auditors report no default in repayment of loans to banks or financial institutions and no cash losses in the year [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.65][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.66].

## SME listing
- The company was listed on NSE Emerge on August 11, 2025, and as an SME-listed entity is exempt from mandatory IND-AS adoption [Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.34][Bhadora Industries Annual Report p.23].

On behalf of the Board of Directors, I extend my heartfelt gratitude for your continued support, trust, and encouragement that has enabled our Company to progress with strength and resilience. I take this moment to thank all our shareholders, employees, bankers, advisors, and well-wishers who played a vital role in making this possible.

answer:
## Short answer
On the disclosed metrics, **Inox Wind carries by far the biggest group-contagion risk relative to size**: 64.74% of its loans and advances in FY2025-26 (44% in FY2024-25) went to related parties, and 12.88–26% of sales were to related parties, against consolidated revenue of ₹4,397.51 crore in FY2025-26 [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.153][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.279][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.69]. **Refex** is the opposite — related-party sales were 0.08% of total sales in FY2025-26 and loans/advances to related parties 0%, though it carries large corporate guarantees for subsidiaries [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.145][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261]. **Metal Coatings** and **GRM Overseas** disclose only ordinary-course RPTs with limited quantitative loan/guarantee exposure in the evidence.

## Refex Industries
- Share of RPTs: sales to related parties 0.08% of total sales in FY2025-26 (0.35% in FY2024-25); purchases NA / 0.07%; loans & advances to related parties 0% in FY2025-26 and 100% in FY2024-25 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.145].
- No loans or advances to firms/companies in which directors were interested, except loans to subsidiaries/wholly-owned subsidiaries [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.127].
- Section 186 disclosures: loans & advances to subsidiaries ₹8,277.50 lakh (Refex Green Mobility) and ₹3,697.00 lakh (Venwind Refex Power); corporate guarantees ₹5,231.45 lakh (Refex Green Mobility), ₹45,706.00 lakh (Venwind Refex Power) and ₹3,748.00 lakh (other companies) as at 31 March 2026 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261].
- Loans to subsidiaries carry 9% interest; unutilised preferential-issue funds placed as ICDs with Rudra Securities at 11% [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.224].
- Size: consolidated turnover ₹2,412 crore and consolidated PAT ₹204 crore in FY2025-26 [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.56].

## Inox Wind
- Sales to related parties were 12.88% of total sales in FY2025-26 and 26% in FY2024-25; loans & advances to related parties 64.74% of total loans & advances in FY2025-26 and 44% in FY2024-25; investments in related parties 0% in both years [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.153].
- Loans/advances in the nature of loans repayable on demand to related parties aggregated ₹2,11,663.40 lakh, unsecured, carrying 7.50%–12% p.a. [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.187][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.251].
- Guarantees aggregating ₹135 crore were provided in favour of banks/financial institutions for facilities availed by IGESL as on 30 June 2026 [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.71].
- No guarantees received or provided for any related-party receivables or payables; a doubtful ICD expense of ₹1,346 lakh was recognised [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.238][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.342].
- Size: consolidated revenue from operations ₹4,39,751.76 lakh (₹4,397.12 crore) in FY2025-26 vs ₹3,55,714.75 lakh in FY2024-25 [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.279][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.69].

## Metal Coatings
- Related-party transactions during FY2025-26 were at arm's length, in the ordinary course, and included material RPTs with M/s Khandelwal Busar Industries Private Limited (KBIPL) [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.14][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.116].
- The related-party relationship with KBIPL arises solely on account of common promoter control; no cross-shareholding either way [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.137].
- Proposed RPT amount totalling ₹95 crore, around 64% of the preceding year's annual consolidated turnover; KBIPL's own turnover ₹7,028.27 lakh, PAT ₹240.58 lakh, net worth ₹3,235.12 lakh [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.138].
- The proposed transaction does not involve any loans, inter-corporate deposits, advances or investments by the Company [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.140].
- Size: total equity ₹4,397.00 lakh as at 31 March 2026; total borrowings ₹352.11 lakh [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110].

## GRM Overseas
- Material RPTs proposed with GRM Foodkraft Private Limited (91.48% owned) up to ₹600 crore, equal to 44.52% of consolidated turnover and 111.31% of Foodkraft's standalone turnover [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.254].
- RPTs with Eros Agro & Farms Private Limited of up to ₹750 crore per financial year, 55.65% of consolidated turnover, structured as an unsecured loan at 8% repayable on demand [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.261].
- RPTs with GRM International Holdings Ltd, UK of up to ₹75 crore (5.56% of consolidated turnover) [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.257][GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.256].
- Borrowings include inter-corporate loans ₹5,218.76 lakh and loans from related parties ₹4,026.34 lakh, carrying 7% interest [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.213].
- Corporate guarantee for subsidiary loan disclosed as nil [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.224][GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.171].
- Size: consolidated revenue from operations ₹1,34,819.28 lakh, PAT ₹6,123.63 lakh in FY2024-25 [GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.189].

## Relative group-contagion risk
- Inox Wind's related-party dependence is highest on both the asset (64.74% of loans & advances) and revenue (12.88%) side relative to its ₹4,397 crore turnover, and it adds ₹135 crore of guarantees for IGESL [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.153][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.69][Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.71].
- Refex's RPT shares are minimal (0.08% sales, 0% loans) but its ₹54,685.45 lakh of corporate guarantees for subsidiaries is large versus its ₹2,412 crore turnover [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.145][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.261][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.56].
- Metal Coatings and GRM Overseas show material RPT volumes but little disclosed related-party loan/guarantee exposure beyond GRM's related-party borrowings, which are modest against its ₹1,348 crore revenue [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.140][GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.213][GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025 p.189].

answer:
## Short answer
Gammon India is in acute distress: NPA since June 2017, loans recalled, lender resolution plan unconcluded, penal interest of about ₹911.54 crore disputed and not accounted, standalone loss of ₹1,189 crore, and a qualified audit opinion citing going-concern uncertainty [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.72][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.44][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.121][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.82][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.67][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143]. Refex carries GST penalties and income-tax demands in the low crores against revenue of ₹2,075 crore standalone and PAT of ₹246 crore [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.144][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.323][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55]. Infosys's proceedings are tax claims and ordinary-course litigation, immaterial against ₹1,78,650 crore consolidated revenue and ₹29,440 crore consolidated net profit [infosys-ar-26 p.344][infosys-ar-26 p.345][infosys-ar-26 p.333][infosys-ar-26 p.81].

## Refex Industries
- Ongoing legal proceedings include criminal, tax, statutory/regulatory actions and other material pending litigation; adverse outcomes could affect profitability and financial condition [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.320][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.238].
- Contingent liabilities for direct/indirect tax litigation and third-party claims are a Key Audit Matter; auditors found the estimation and disclosures adequate [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.184][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.267].
- GST assessment orders alleging wrongful input tax credit utilisation: total penalty ₹9,98,64,079, with appeals pending before the Commissioner of Central Tax (Appeals), Mysore, and the Commissioner (Appeal) of Customs & Indirect Taxes, Raipur, among others [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.144].
- Income-tax demands under appeal: ₹4,086.66 lakh (AY2020-21) and ₹1,136.78 lakh after rectification (AY2021-22); a further ₹4,628.17 lakh demand (AY2019-20) is pending before CIT(A) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.323][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324].
- An AY2018-19 demand of ₹72.31 lakh is under a writ petition; a GST demand (July 2017–March 2019) comprises tax of ₹356.46 lakh plus equal penalty, with a GSTAT appeal to be filed [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324].
- A prior ₹3,567.21 lakh demand (AY2016-17) was nullified by a favourable order on 28 April 2026, following an interim stay from the Madras High Court [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324].
- Materiality: standalone turnover ₹2,075 crore and PAT ₹246 crore; consolidated turnover ₹2,412 crore and PAT ₹204 crore [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.56]. The quantified exposures are small relative to these earnings.

## Gammon India
- Lenders' facilities became Non-Performing Assets in June 2017 and all loans were recalled; no new working capital limit was sanctioned during the year [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.72].
- The company entered CDR; lenders approved an SDR scheme in November 2015 converting part of debt into equity (lenders held about 62% of GIL); an ICA was executed in 2019 under the RBI circular of 7 June 2019 [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.3].
- The resolution plan/one-time settlement remains unconcluded: some lenders gave in-principle sanction, the Everstone fund closed, top management of some lenders disagreed, and more than 50% of debt has been assigned to asset reconstruction companies [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.24].
- Penal interest and charges of ₹107.90 crore were charged in FY2025-26; cumulative disputed penal interest is ₹391.76 crore, plus ₹519.78 crore levied by CFM Assets Reconstruction Company; the aggregate contingent amount not accounted is ₹911.54 crore [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.44][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.121].
- Regulatory consequences: directors disqualified under Section 164(2)(b) for NCD redemption default exceeding one year; BSE compulsory delisting order; trading in equity shares suspended; winding-up petitions filed by some creditors; embargo on assets by some bankers [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.63][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143].
- Delays in filing e-forms with the ROC during FY2025-26 were observed [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.63]. Auditor remuneration to one executive director was paid without the lenders' NOC, contrary to Section 197 [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.146].
- Financial position: standalone revenue nil and loss after tax ₹1,189.01 crore [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.82]; current liabilities exceed current assets by ₹14,154.27 crore; qualified audit opinion [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.67]. Auditors cite material going-concern uncertainty; the resolution plan is pending and lenders cannot reach consensus [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.205].

## Infosys
- Consolidated contingent liabilities: claims not acknowledged as debts, with India income-tax matters of ₹1,964 crore; management expects its position to be upheld with no material adverse effect [infosys-ar-26 p.344].
- Standalone income-tax claims were ₹1,326 crore [infosys-ar-26 p.262].
- Fiscal 2026 orders under Sections 250 and 254 confirmed the company's tax position for AY2013-14 and AY2017-18 to 2021-22: interest income (pre-tax) of ₹381 crore recognised, income-tax provision of ₹869 crore reversed, and ₹86 crore reduced from contingent liabilities [infosys-ar-26 p.79][infosys-ar-26 p.329].
- Ordinary-course legal actions are expected, when concluded, not to have a material adverse effect [infosys-ar-26 p.345]. No undisputed statutory dues were in arrears for more than six months [infosys-ar-26 p.204].
- Materiality: consolidated revenue ₹1,78,650 crore and consolidated net profit ₹29,440 crore [infosys-ar-26 p.333][infosys-ar-26 p.81]; consolidated cash and investments ₹43,075 crore with no outstanding borrowings [infosys-ar-26 p.80].

## Comparison
- Nature: Gammon's issues are lender-driven insolvency/resolution and regulatory default; Refex's are GST and income-tax assessments under appeal; Infosys's are tax claims and ordinary-course litigation [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.3][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.144][infosys-ar-26 p.344].
- Quantified exposure: Gammon about ₹911.54 crore of disputed penal interest not accounted, versus a standalone loss of ₹1,189.01 crore and negative current position of ₹14,154.27 crore — material and going-concern relevant [Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.121][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.82][Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon p.143]. Refex's largest demand is ₹4,628.17 lakh against PAT of ₹246 crore [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.324][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.55]; Infosys's largest is ₹1,964 crore of income-tax claims against net profit of ₹29,440 crore [infosys-ar-26 p.344][infosys-ar-26 p.81].

chunks.text: Every Industry/Sector has its ups and downs. Gammon is also subject to such vulnerability and it has affected its performance post 2013 due to economic recession and certain shift in policies. The Company had posted major losses for the 1st time after nearly 80 years and giving constant dividend for approx. 40 years to shareholders. Pursuant to the inability of Gammon to repay its lenders the Company was admitted to the Corporate Debt Restructuring (‘CDR’). Thereafter in November 2015, lenders approved the scheme of corporate realignment and SDR. Under SDR, a part of debt was converted into equity thereby giving lenders approx. 62% equity stake in GIL. Further pursuant to RBI Circular dated 7th June, 2019, all the lenders of the Company executed an Inter-creditor Agreement (ICA) in 2019. Post execution of the ICA the Company submitted its draft resolution plan to the lenders including restructuring and change in ownership. The resolution plan/ one time settlement is in its advanced stages, and the company is confident to receive approval from the lenders shortly. With the new investor investing further funds in the company, the company will soon revive as an EPC Company. Gammon continued to hold strategic Italy-based Sofinter Group. The Group is engaged in the engineering, procurement and construction of steam and power generation boilers, water and waste treatment and flameless combustion technology with application in oil & gas, power generation and industrial sector. Sofinter S.p.A., A.C. Boilers S.p.A (for Ansaldo Calaie S.p.A)., ITEA and Europower are some companies under the Group. The Company has a substantial stake in Puma Oil Block in the Oriente basin in Eucador Prevailing cash flow constraints has affected international business too.

## Short answer
Refex's rating symbols are not disclosed in the evidence, so no comparison is possible.

## CEAT
- CARE reaffirmed long-term 'AA' with 'Positive' outlook (also extended to proposed NCDs) and short-term/CP at 'A1+'; Ind-Ra affirmed 'AA'/Positive and 'A1+' on CP [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.61].
- The reaffirmation explicitly considered the increase in long-term debt to fund expansions and the CAMSO acquisition [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.61].
- Debt-Equity rose from 0.45 to 0.59 (+33.82%) due to higher short and long-term borrowings [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.131].
- DSCR improved to 1.89 from 1.73; ROE rose to 17% from 12% on higher profit [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.131].
- ROCE rose to 21.46% from 16.48% [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.132]; gearing (net debt basis) rose to 37% from 31%, with no covenant breaches [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.130].
- Consolidated net profit ₹69,724 lakh vs ₹47,137 lakh; EBITDA ₹2,06,300 lakh, up 38% [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re p.45].

## Inox Wind
- Long-term bank facilities upgraded from 'A+' to 'AA-'; short-term continued at 'A1+', the highest rating [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.134].
- Company states it remains net cash positive as on Mar'26 and cites AA- (long-term)/A1+ (short-term) [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.50].
- Debt-Equity improved (down 33%) on reduced debt and higher net worth; current ratio up 26% [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.53].
- Interest-bearing debt and NCRPS/NCPRPS were eliminated via a ₹1,249 crore rights issue and the IWEL merger, giving net cash positive [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.54].
- Consolidated revenue grew 23%, EBITDA and Cash PAT more than 25%; merger cut liabilities by ~₹2,050 crore [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.7].
- Watch: auditor flags revenue recognition and ECL on trade receivables as key audit matters, with receivables mainly from state-owned enterprises [Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026 p.181].

## Refex Industries
- Acuité reaffirmed the bank loan facility ratings by letter dated January 08, 2026, but the rating symbols themselves are not shown in the evidence [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.76][Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.121].
- Debt-Equity decreased due to higher shareholders' equity; DSCR increased on higher current earnings; current ratio declined on higher current liabilities [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.259].
- Net debt is nil, with cash and cash equivalents (₹18,370.81 lakh) exceeding total debt (₹16,210.73 lakh) [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.333].
- Watch: contingent liabilities/tax litigation are a key audit matter with high judgement [Refex Industries Annual Report FY 202526 p.184].

## Metal Coatings
- Acuité reaffirmed 'ACUITE BBB' long-term and 'A3+' short-term with 'Stable' outlook on January 22, 2026 [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.10]; same ratings reaffirmed in FY2024-25 [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2025 p.9].
- DSCR jumped to 211.18x from 2.24x on lower interest cost; interest coverage 227.02x vs 2.30x [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38].
- Debt-Equity rose to 0.08 from 0.04 on increased debt, still very low [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110][Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.38].
- Total borrowings ₹352.11 lakh vs equity ₹4,397.00 lakh [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110]; no default on interest or loan repayment [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.10].
- Current ratio 4.49x; ROE 5.57% [Metal Coatings Annual Report FY 2026 p.110].

chunks.section: Revenue Recognition and Impairment of Trade Receivables
chunks.text: Revenue is recognised when the control of the underlying products has been transferred to the customer. We have identified recognition of revenue as a key audit matter as revenue is a key performance indicator. There is presumed fraud risk of revenue being overstated during the year on account of variation in the timing of the transfer of control due to pressure to achieve performance targets and meeting external expectations. Trade receivables are mainly comprised of receivables from state government-owned enterprises and private dealers. We have identified the impairment of trade receivables as a significant audit matter on account of the significant judgment and estimate involved. These factors include the customer’s ability and willingness to pay the outstanding amounts, past due receivables, and financial and economic difficulties of customers. (Refer Note 40 (vii) of the standalone financial statements) This assessment is done for each customer resulting from possible defaults over the expected life of the receivables. Based on this assessment, the credit loss rate is determined in the provision matrix. The credit loss rate is based on the experience of actual credit losses over past years adjusted to reflect the current economic conditions and forecasts of future economic conditions. Based on such credit loss rate, the company recorded expected credit loss (ECL) allowance for trade receivable. In view of this, we have considered the measurement of ECL on trade receivables as a key audit matter. ## Short answer
In 2026 the expanded risk-based approach remains optional for non-Category I/II firms, but the agencies estimate such a firm could see a 5–10% capital-requirement reduction by opting in [91fr14952 p.149].

## Classification and framework
- Category IV applies to banking organizations with at least $100bn in total assets that do not meet Category III thresholds [91fr14952 p.3]. Mandatory expanded risk-based approach (credit, equity, operational, market, CVA) is limited to Category I and II firms [91fr14952 p.6][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.1].
- In 2023 the expanded risk-based approach used standardized methodologies for credit, equity and operational risk; internal models remained permitted for market risk with supervisory approval [gsib-memo-change-summary p.4][91fr14952 p.5]. The advanced approaches were removed; the standardized approach ceases to apply to Category I/II firms [91fr14952 p.5].
- The 2026 package keeps mandatory expanded risk-based approach for Category I/II only; all other organizations have the option to adopt it [fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.1][gsib-memo-change-summary p.2]. Market risk framework applies to others only with significant trading activity (>$5bn or ≥10% of assets) [91fr14952 p.5][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.2].

## AOCI / unrealised securities gains and losses
- Under the 2023 proposal, a firm opting into the expanded risk-based approach would become subject to the Category I/II definition of capital and would have to reflect most elements of AOCI in regulatory capital, losing the opt-out [91fr14952 p.6][91fr14952 p.11][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.8]. Non-opting firms kept the AOCI opt-out [91fr14952 p.352].
- 2026: the proposed AOCI transition begins January 1, 2027, for expanded-approach users that had an AOCI opt-out effective December 31, 2026, phasing the AOCI adjustment in over five years (2027–2032) [91fr14952 p.356][91fr14952 p.377][91fr14952 p.336]. Agencies estimate AOCI inclusion raises Category III/IV CET1 requirements by 3.1% [board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.12].

## Buffers and leverage
- GSIB surcharge applies only to GSIBs; a $150bn regional is not a GSIB [91fr14952 p.351][91fr14952 p.3].
- Stress capital buffer: Category I buffers include SCB, CCyB and GSIB surcharge; Category II SCB plus CCyB; subsidiary depository institutions 2.5% plus CCyB [91fr14952 p.7].
- 2026 package extends the countercyclical capital buffer and supplementary leverage ratio requirements to Category IV firms [gsib-memo-change-summary p.6].

## Net capital effect
- 2023: opting in would cut a below-Category IV firm's requirements by 5–10% (a third of firms), with only a small number above 10%; three Category III/IV holding companies would see 3–7% reductions [91fr14952 p.149].
- 2026: the standardized approach proposal lowers Category III/IV CET1 requirements 3.0%, or 5.2% with stress-test changes; below $100bn, 7.8% [board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.12][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.13][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.3].

## Opting in
- Any banking organization may adopt the expanded risk-based approach in its entirety; it then becomes subject to the same capital definition as Category I/II, including most AOCI, and SA-CCR, which may deter smaller firms [91fr14952 p.6][91fr14952 p.149]. Firms becoming Category I/II later are bound by it [91fr14952 p.149].

The agencies estimate that three Category III or IV holding companies would see a reduction in capital requirements in the range of three to seven percent if they were to choose to apply the expanded risk-based approach instead of the concurrently proposed revised standardized approach. In addition, the agencies estimate that about a third of banking organizations below Category IV would see reductions in capital requirements of between five and ten percent if they were to apply the expanded risk-based approach, although only a small number might see a reduction in capital requirements greater than ten percent. However, various features of the expanded risk-based approach that are appropriate for larger and more complex banking organizations, such as the requirements to adopt SA–CCR and reflect most elements of accumulated other comprehensive income in regulatory capital, may make the framework unappealing to many smaller banking organizations. Section VIII.F.2 considers further how other banking organizations’ may respond to the optional application of this rule. Lastly, while banking organizations that remain below the Category I and II applicability thresholds would retain this optionality, those that subsequently become Category I or II banking organizations would become subject to the proposal’s requirements. These banking organizations present substantial systemic risks due to their size, complexity, interconnectedness, and cross-jurisdictional activity. Application of the expanded risk-based approach to them would provide granular, risk-sensitive, and standardized requirements that align with international standards. Therefore, the proposal would provide all banking organizations subject to the capital rule with the option of adopting the expanded risk-based approach in its entirety. chunks.text: > The proposal would streamline the risk-based capital requirements for large banking organizations. Category I and II banking organizations would be subject to a single set of risk-based capital ratio requirements based on the “expanded risk-based approach,” which would include requirements for credit risk, operational risk, market risk, and CVA risk. chunks.text: The risk-based capital proposal would introduce the expanded risk-based approach, which includes risk-weighted assets for credit, equity, operational, market, and credit valuation adjustment risk. The proposed risk-weighting methodologies would be standardized (except for market risk, for which use of internal models would still be allowed subject to enhanced supervisory standards) to improve consistency of requirements across banks and over time. The expanded risk-based approach would be more risk-sensitive than the current standardized approach by incorporating more credit-risk drivers (for example, borrower and loan characteristics) and explicitly differentiating between more types of risk (for example, operational risk). In this manner, the expanded risk-based approach would better account for key risks faced by large firms. The expanded risk-based approach would replace the Board’s internal models-based capital requirements for credit and operational risk in the current advanced approaches. Internal models used in this context rely on a firm’s choice of modeling assumptions and include a degree of subjectivity, which in supervisors’ experience can result in unwarranted variability in requirements for exposures with similar risks. The variability and complexity of these models- based approaches can reduce the transparency of the capital ratios, challenge comparisons of

As part of the revised market risk framework, the proposal would include a risk-sensitive and consistent framework for capturing the risks associated with credit valuation adjustment risk for derivative exposures.19This framework would apply to (1) Category I and II depository institution holding companies, (2) depository institutions that are subsidiaries of Category I or II depository institution holding companies and have significant trading activity, and (3) other banking organizations with significant trading activity that also have at least $1 trillion in notional derivative exposure. The proposal would retain banking organizations’ ability to use internal models, with supervisory approval, to calculate market risk capital requirements. Market risk is more effectively modeled than credit and operational risk because relevant data is observed at a much higher frequency and depth, providing the basis for both model calibration and empirical verification of model appropriateness. The agencies consider the proposed requirements under the expanded risk- based approach to be appropriate for Category I and II banking organizations given their risk profiles, complexity, risk management resources, and international activities. The agencies recognize that the risk-sensitive requirements under the expanded risk- based approach may appeal to other banking organizations with certain business models and risk management systems. Therefore, the proposal would allow other banking organizations to elect to use the expanded risk-based approach. Banking organizations that choose this option would also be subject to the definition of capital that applies to Category I and II banking organizations.20

Currently, these banking organizations are subject to two sets of risk-based capital ratio requirements: one based on the standardized approach (which also generally applies to other banking organizations) and the other based on an internal models framework, the advanced approaches.17Under the proposal, Category I and II banking organizations would be subject to a single set of risk-based capital ratio requirements based on the ‘‘expanded risk-based approach’’—which would include requirements for credit risk, equity risk, and operational risk—and the revised market risk framework.18 The standardized approach would no longer apply to these banking organizations, and the advanced approaches would be removed from the regulatory capital framework. As discussed further below, other banking organizations could choose to adopt the expanded risk-based approach that would be required for Category I and II banking organizations. The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (collectively, the agencies) issued three proposals on March 19, 2026, to modernize the regulatory capital framework for banking organizations of all sizes. These proposals result from a comprehensive, bottom-up review of the capital framework, which aims to ensure individual requirements are appropriate and do not result in unintended effects. In analyzing the effects of the proposals, the agencies considered overlaps among requirements and sought to mitigate them where appropriate. The first proposal would streamline the risk-based capital requirements for Category I and II depository institution holding companies and depository institutions (Category I and II banking organizations) by requiring them to calculate only one set of risk-based capital ratios using the “expanded risk-based approach,” which would include requirements for credit risk, operational risk, market risk, and credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk. All other banking organizations would have the option to adopt this proposed approach. The proposal would also apply the market risk framework to banking organizations with significant trading activities. The second proposal would revise the capital treatment of certain exposure categories under the standardized approach by improving the calibration and risk sensitivity of risk weights that are particularly material to covered banking organizations’ lending activities while maintaining the simplicity of the standardized approach.

•The two proposals for public comment would improve the comprehensiveness, consistency, and transparency of the capital requirements applicable to large banking firms. •The first proposal would replace the agencies’ risk-based capital framework for large firms with a new framework consistent with standards issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. The proposal would: oApply to firms with at least $100 billion in total assets and to their depository institution subsidiaries; its market risk provisions would also apply to smaller firms with significant trading activities; oReduce the ability of firms to use internal models for measuring capital requirements, as such models can result in unwarranted variation in requirements across firms; oRequire firms to use more risk-sensitive standardized approaches to ensure appropriate capitalization for credit, market, and operational risk exposures, while limiting variation in capital requirements across firms; and oNot change capital requirements for smaller, less complex firms. •The second proposal would revise the calculation of the GSIB risk-based capital surcharge to ensure that the surcharge is more reflective of a GSIB’s systemic risk profile. •The changes to capital requirements under the two proposals would increase the resilience of large firms and enhance financial stability. oMore appropriate capitalization of certain risks would increase overall capital requirements. The impact on capital requirements derives mostly from the first proposal, which would increase common equity tier 1 capital requirements for large firms by an estimated 16 percent. Additional elements of the proposal could lead to a further moderate increase in requirements for some firms over the long run,

chunks.section: Application of the new risk-based capital framework to all large firms
chunks.text: The expanded risk-based approach would apply to firms with total assets of $100 billion or more and their subsidiary depository institutions.4 This approach would provide more risk- sensitive and consistent requirements, which better account for the risks of these firms. The Board had previously determined that the burden of the internal models-based advanced approaches requirements exceeded the benefits for firms subject to Category III or IV capital standards. The expanded risk-based approach would be much less complex and burdensome to implement than the advanced approaches and, as a result, the proposal would apply the expanded risk-based approach to all large firms. The proposal would also align the calculation of regulatory capital for firms subject to Category III or IV capital standards with the calculation for firms subject to Category I or II capital standards, providing a single approach for large firms. Among other items, firms subject to Category III or IV standards would be required to reflect accumulated other comprehensive income in regulatory capital, which would better reflect their capacity to absorb losses. To further align capital requirements across large firms and enhance the resilience of firms subject to Category IV standards, the proposal would extend the countercyclical capital buffer and the supplementary leverage ratio requirements to firms subject to Category IV standards. 4 In addition, the revised requirements for market risk would apply to any firm with $5 billion or more in trading assets plus trading liabilities or for which trading assets plus trading liabilities equal 10 percent or more of the firm’s total assets.

with the proposed revisions to stress testing models, the common equity tier 1 capital requirements of Category III and IV firms are projected to decrease by 5.2 percent. answer:
## Short answer
Basel's global framework treats mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as a "threshold deduction" item: amounts are deducted from CET1 above a 10% individual cap and above a 15% aggregate cap with other specified items, with non-deducted amounts risk-weighted at 250% [BaselFramework p.164][BaselFramework p.300][BaselFramework p.165]. Current US rules apply this deduction framework only to Category I and II banking organizations, exempting smaller ones [91fr14952 p.186][91fr14952 p.11]. The 2026 proposals would remove the MSR deduction altogether, subjecting all MSAs to a 250% risk weight [91fr14952 p.5][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.2][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.3], to eliminate a disincentive to mortgage servicing and partly reverse migration of mortgage activity to nonbanks [91fr14952 p.5][91fr14952 p.195][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.13].

## Basel treatment
- MSRs, significant investments in unconsolidated financials, and temporary-difference DTAs may each receive limited recognition capped at 10% of CET1 after applicable adjustments [BaselFramework p.164].
- The aggregate of the three items remaining after the 10% treatment must not exceed 15% of CET1; excess is deducted via the 17.65% calculation [BaselFramework p.164][BaselFramework p.165].
- Amounts below the deduction thresholds receive a 250% risk weight rather than a deduction [BaselFramework p.300][BaselFramework p.165].
- Goodwill and other intangibles are fully deducted, with MSRs explicitly excepted from that full-deduction rule [BaselFramework p.142].

## Current US rules by bank size
- Category I and II banking organizations must deduct MSAs from CET1 when they exceed 10% of CET1 individually or 15% in aggregate with other threshold items; non-deducted portions get a 250% risk weight [91fr14952 p.186][91fr14952 p.11].
- Smaller organizations are not subject to this MSA deduction requirement — the threshold-based deduction applies to large firms [91fr14952 p.186][91fr14952 p.11].
- The 10%/15% deduction framework is codified for Category I/II institutions (and those using expanded total RWAs) [91fr14952 p.354][91fr14952 p.334].

## 2026 proposals: what would change
- Proposals issued March 19, 2026 would eliminate the MSR threshold deduction and apply a 250% risk weight to all MSAs, consistent with the current treatment for MSAs below the thresholds [91fr14952 p.5][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.2][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.3].
- The standardized approach proposal would remove the threshold-based deduction for all banking organizations, including community bank leverage ratio filers [fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.3][91fr14952 p.199].
- The 250% risk weight is retained, acknowledging MSR interest-rate sensitivity and valuation uncertainty [91fr14952 p.186][91fr14952 p.11].
- No Category I or II organization currently carries an above-threshold MSR deduction, though removing the treatment could still significantly affect origination and servicing incentives [91fr14952 p.148].

## Rationale and migration concern
- The change would eliminate a strong disincentive to mortgage origination and servicing and support the housing market [91fr14952 p.5][91fr14952 p.4].
- Post-crisis reforms contributed to migration of mortgage origination and servicing outside the regulated banking sector [91fr14952 p.5][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.4].
- Nonbank mortgage companies originated about two-thirds of US mortgages and held servicing rights on 54% of balances in 2022, versus 39% of originations and 4% of servicing in 2008 [91fr14952 p.5].
- The proposal could partially reverse migration to nonbanks, supporting bank competitiveness and financial stability [91fr14952 p.195][board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.13][91fr14952 p.196].

## GSIB surcharge interaction
- GSIB surcharge and systemic-indicator proposals are separate; risk-weighted assets feed the current method 2 short-term wholesale funding score, so lower RWAs can partly offset capital effects in GSIB surcharges [91fr14952 p.164][91fr14952 p.199].
- The proposal would modify method 2 coefficients, remove the RWA denominator from the short-term wholesale funding indicator, and average systemic indicators over the year [board-memo-basel-gsib-standardized-appro p.8][fact-sheet-SUMMARY p.4].

However, in some cases, these post-crisis reforms have imposed burdens that contributed to the migration of some activities, such as mortgage origination and servicing, outside of the regulated banking sector.16Revising the regulatory capital framework to better align requirements with risks—and in so doing easing requirements on some lower-risk, traditional banking activities—would contribute to U.S. banking organizations becoming better positioned to support the economy. C. Overview of the Proposal The proposal would streamline the risk-based capital requirements applicable to Category I and II banking organizations. Currently, these banking organizations are subject to two sets of risk-based capital ratio requirements: one based on the standardized approach (which also generally applies to other banking organizations) and the other based on an internal models framework, the advanced approaches.17Under the proposal, Category I and II banking organizations would be subject to a single set of risk-based capital ratio requirements based on the ‘‘expanded risk-based approach’’—which would include requirements for credit risk, equity risk, and operational risk—and the revised market risk framework.18 The standardized approach would no longer apply to these banking organizations, and the advanced approaches would be removed from the regulatory capital framework. As discussed further below, other banking organizations could choose to adopt the expanded risk-based approach that would be required for Category I and II banking organizations. The expanded risk-based approach is a standardized framework that would promote the simplicity, risk sensitivity, transparency, and consistency objectives of the proposal. This approach would improve risk sensitivity

mortgage servicing assets deduction treatment could also make mortgage lending relationships under these types of models more attractive, particularly for Ginnie Mae securitizations where lenders must pool together multiple loans themselves. 3. On Nonbank Financial Intermediaries The proposal would likely drive expansion in bank lending that could partially reverse the ongoing migration of activity to the nonbank financial sector in a manner that could support financial stability. Heightened capital requirements have been identified as one factor in nonbanks’ increased share of financial market activity. The proposal reduces requirements in certain areas, particularly for traditional lending activities such as mortgages and corporate loans, in a way that would support bank competitiveness relative to nonbanks. Given the greater willingness and capacity for lending that banks demonstrate during periods of stress, this could generate stability benefits.

Taken together, the Basel III proposal and the GSIB surcharge proposal would better align capital requirements for the largest banking organizations with risks. The current framework includes multiple components (two leverage ratios, the stress capital buffer, the GSIB surcharge, and traditional risk-based capital with multiple sets of calculations), which introduce substantial complexity to firms’ capital planning and result in deadweight costs. Despite the moderate reduction in capital requirements these proposals would cause, a simpler and more transparent capital framework produced by the proposals would increase the efficiency of capital allocation in a risk-sensitive manner and retain the resilience of large banking organizations. The proposed changes to the standardized approach would revise certain risk weights applicable to non-Category I and II firms to more closely reflect the underlying risks. These changes would lower the capital required by these firms to support certain traditional lending activities, including mortgages. In particular, these revisions are expected to support on-balance sheet lending by these banks, potentially reversing some of the migration in activity to non-banks that has occurred over the past decade. Given the key role that bank lending plays in supporting overall economic activity, these changes are expected to generate significant economic benefits.

FAQ This FAQ is meant to clarify the calculation of the 15% limit on significant investments in the common shares of unconsolidated financial institutions (banks, insurance and other financial entities); mortgage servicing rights, and DTAs arising from temporary differences (collectively referred to as specified items). The recognition of these specified items will be limited to 15% of Common Equity Tier 1 capital, after the application of all deductions. To determine the maximum amount of the specified items that can be recognised*, banks and supervisors should multiply the amount of Common Equity Tier 1** (after all deductions, including after the deduction of the specified items in full) by 17.65%. This number is derived from the proportion of 15% to 85% (ie 15%/85% = 17.65%). As an example, take a bank with €85 of common equity (calculated net of all deductions, including after the deduction of the specified items in full). The maximum amount of specified items that can be recognised by this bank in its calculation of Common Equity Tier 1 capital is €85 x 17.65% = €15. Any excess above €15 must be deducted from Common Equity Tier 1. If the bank has specified items (excluding amounts deducted after applying the individual 10% limits) that in aggregate sum up to the 15% limit, Common Equity Tier 1 after inclusion of the specified items, will amount to €85 + €15 = €100. The percentage of specified items to total Common Equity Tier 1 would equal 15%. * The actual amount that will be recognised may be lower than this maximum, either because the sum of the three specified items are below the 15% limit set out in this annex, or due to the application of the 10% limit applied to each item.

Under the capital rule, each GSIB is subject to an additional risk-based capital buffer requirement (GSIB surcharge) to strengthen the firm’s resilience based on the risks its failure or distress could pose to the U.S. financial system. The GSIB surcharge proposal would improve the framework’s measurement of systemic risk and better align surcharges with GSIBs’ systemic risk. The proposal would improve the calculation of GSIB surcharges in several ways. First, the proposal would modify the method 2 fixed coefficients to (1) reflect changes in the financial system and economy over the past few years and (2) introduce a mechanism that would automatically adjust these coefficients annually to account for economic growth and inflation going forward. Second, to better align the surcharge requirement with the systemic risk posed by GSIBs, the proposal would remove the risk-weighted assets denominator from the short-term wholesale funding indicator and recalibrate the indicator’s weighting to 20 percent, as originally intended. Third, to better reflect a firm’s systemic risk profile and reduce incentives for firms to make temporary adjustments to reported indicators of systemic risk at year-end, the proposal would require firms to calculate certain systemic indicators as an annual average of their daily or monthly values rather than on a point-in-time basis at year-end. Fourth, to reduce cliff effects and increase the sensitivity of the GSIB surcharge to changes in a firm’s systemic risk profile, the proposal would assign surcharges in increments of 10 basis points rather than 50 basis points.

The third proposal would modify certain aspects of the U.S. standardized approach to improve risk sensitivity while generally maintaining the simplicity of the current framework. The proposal would better calibrate capital requirements for the risks of the largest categories of bank lending activities, moderately reducing them relative to the current standardized approach. For example, the proposal would use loan-to-value ratios to determine the applicable risk weight for residential real estate exposures. In addition, the proposal would make targeted adjustments to the existing counterparty credit risk, credit risk mitigation and securitization frameworks, which align with those included in the Basel III proposal. Together, these changes aim to retain simple and robust requirements while helping banks further support lending to the economy. Both the standardized approach proposal and the Basel III proposal would remove any requirement to deduct mortgage servicing assets from regulatory capital and would instead assign a 250 percent risk weight to all such assets (while also asking a question about the appropriate risk weight for these assets).10 This change would help promote bank participation in mortgage businesses, while recognizing uncertainty regarding firms’ ability to realize value from mortgage servicing assets over the economic cycle. The standardized approach proposal would also require Category III and IV firms to include elements of accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) in common equity tier 1 10 This proposed modification to the definition of capital would apply to all banking organizations subject to the capital rule, including those subject to community bank leverage ratio framework.

The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (collectively, the agencies) issued three proposals on March 19, 2026, to modernize the regulatory capital framework for banking organizations of all sizes. These proposals result from a comprehensive, bottom-up review of the capital framework, which aims to ensure individual requirements are appropriate and do not result in unintended effects. In analyzing the effects of the proposals, the agencies considered overlaps among requirements and sought to mitigate them where appropriate. The first proposal would streamline the risk-based capital requirements for Category I and II depository institution holding companies and depository institutions (Category I and II banking organizations) by requiring them to calculate only one set of risk-based capital ratios using the “expanded risk-based approach,” which would include requirements for credit risk, operational risk, market risk, and credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk. All other banking organizations would have the option to adopt this proposed approach. The proposal would also apply the market risk framework to banking organizations with significant trading activities. The second proposal would revise the capital treatment of certain exposure categories under the standardized approach by improving the calibration and risk sensitivity of risk weights that are particularly material to covered banking organizations’ lending activities while maintaining the simplicity of the standardized approach.

An overall moderate lowering of required capital for Category I and II banking organizations, moving closer in line with the requirements for internationally active foreign banks, could somewhat increase U.S. banking organizations’ ability to compete for business internationally. Lower risk weights relative to the current standardized approach in certain lending areas could advantage covered banking organizations in attracting domestic customers, though other changes, like ending capital deduction for excess mortgage servicing assets, could also help them support smaller banking organizations through correspondence lending relationships, growing aggregate lending. At the same time, the concurrent standardized approach proposal and the option available to smaller banking organizations to use the expanded risk- based approach under this proposal would help ensure continued robust competition between domestic banking organizations. The proposal may induce some lower-risk traditional lending activities to flow back into the banking sector in a way that would enhance competition and financial stability in the United States. Finally, the analysis discusses how key lending areas could see improved pricing and service quality as increased competition reduces applicable interest rates, and how regulatory barriers to entry into the largest bank tiers would be reduced through a shift to lower, less complex, and more certain capital requirements.

The proposal would likely, in aggregate, encourage the migration of certain activities, particularly traditional lending, back towards banking organizations while effects on trading activities would be more mixed. Lower risk weights for most mortgages and the removal of the mortgage servicing assets threshold capital deduction could encourage covered banking organizations to maintain or expand these activities relative to nonbank financial intermediaries, directly and via correspondent lending relationships with independent mortgage banks and smaller depository institutions. More broadly, enhanced competition in key lending markets could reduce the premiums that lenders can charge above their costs, providing greater economic benefits to consumers. For Category I and II banking organizations, heterogenous effects on different products within the proposed market risk framework could incentivize liquidity provision for those products to either shift toward or away from nonbank financial intermediaries, with increases in risk weights being offset by both reductions in the GSIB surcharge proposal and the proposed revision to stress test scenarios. A. Overview of the Baseline This section discusses the current state of Category I and II banking organizations and the economy absent the proposal (the baseline) to help understand the potential effects of the proposal. To help contextualize the broader macroeconomic effects of the proposal, a discussion of the total banking system is also included.
